title: OOP & Software Design
goal: Learn where logic belongs and make responsibilities explicit.

topics.title: Responsibility
topics.description: A responsibility is an obligation an object fulfills using information it owns or collaborators it needs.
learningGoals: Each class has a concrete behavioral purpose
The refactor preserves observable rules
examples: BankAccount controls balance and account state.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A responsibility is an obligation an object fulfills using information it owns or collaborators it needs. Start with behavior, then group duties that belong together. A class name is not a justification for its existence.

workedExample.scenario: BankAccount controls balance and account state.
steps: It validates withdrawals.
A use-case coordinator handles loading and saving.

commonMistakes: Creating a class for every noun can fragment one coherent responsibility.
material.independentExercise: Refactor a procedural withdrawal into the smallest useful objects.
recallQuestions: Why does this class exist?
Which duty would not belong here?

acceptanceCriteria: Each class has a concrete behavioral purpose
The refactor preserves observable rules

topics.title: Information expert
topics.description: Place a decision with the object that has the information needed to make it.
learningGoals: The rule is enforced at its state owner
Infrastructure lookup stays outside domain behavior
examples: An account knows balance and frozen state.

tasks.title: Explain Information expert in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Place a decision with the object that has the information needed to make it. This reduces duplicated checks and keeps invariants near their state. Expertise does not require the object to fetch infrastructure data itself.

workedExample.scenario: An account knows balance and frozen state.
steps: withdraw decides whether spending is legal.
The service obtains the account from storage.

commonMistakes: Moving every rule into a service strips the domain object of behavior.
guidedExercise: Keep repository calls outside the entity
material.independentExercise: Assign token expiration and revocation checks to a token model.
recallQuestions: Who owns the facts for this decision?
Does ownership imply database access?

acceptanceCriteria: The rule is enforced at its state owner
Infrastructure lookup stays outside domain behavior

topics.title: Tell, don't ask
topics.description: Tell an object what operation to perform rather than extracting state and reproducing its rules elsewhere.
learningGoals: Mutation rules have one authoritative location
Read-only queries do not expose mutable internals

tasks.title: Explain Tell, don't ask in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Tell an object what operation to perform rather than extracting state and reproducing its rules elsewhere. Queries still have legitimate uses; the goal is to avoid external mutation logic that bypasses invariants.

steps: The account checks balance and frozen state.
No caller sets its balance directly.

commonMistakes: Tell-don't-ask is not a ban on every getter or query.
guidedExercise: Compare a setter-based withdrawal with a behavior method
material.independentExercise: Replace external token state checks with a domain operation that has explicit failure behavior.
recallQuestions: Which query is legitimate?
Which rule is duplicated by the caller?

acceptanceCriteria: Mutation rules have one authoritative location
Read-only queries do not expose mutable internals

topics.title: High cohesion
topics.description: Cohesion measures whether a component's duties support one coherent purpose.
learningGoals: Responsibilities share a clear purpose
Splits remove unrelated duties without excessive fragmentation
examples: Token hashing changes for a different reason than session policy.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Cohesion measures whether a component's duties support one coherent purpose. Keep behavior that uses the same invariants together. Avoid a large utility or manager class that groups unrelated operations merely because they are convenient.

workedExample.scenario: Token hashing changes for a different reason than session policy.
steps: Keep cryptographic operations separate.
Keep token-state rules together.

commonMistakes: A small class is not necessarily cohesive if its methods are unrelated.
material.independentExercise: Split an account-and-email manager without creating one class per method.
recallQuestions: Which duties belong together?
What change should affect this component?

acceptanceCriteria: Responsibilities share a clear purpose
Splits remove unrelated duties without excessive fragmentation

topics.title: Low coupling
topics.description: Coupling is the knowledge one part has about another.
learningGoals: The caller does not depend on storage layout
The contract expresses use-case needs

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Coupling is the knowledge one part has about another. Depend on the smallest useful behavior rather than internal fields or storage details. Some coupling is necessary; remove knowledge that makes unrelated changes propagate.

steps: It does not construct SQL.
A repository implementation handles query details.

commonMistakes: Adding interfaces everywhere does not automatically reduce meaningful coupling.
guidedExercise: List what the token use case knows
material.independentExercise: Replace direct table access with a repository contract justified by two callers or testing needs.
recallQuestions: What change propagates through this dependency?
What knowledge can the caller avoid?

acceptanceCriteria: The caller does not depend on storage layout
The contract expresses use-case needs

topics.title: Composition
topics.description: Composition builds behavior by delegating to collaborators.
learningGoals: Delegation relationships are explicit
Inheritance is justified by substitutability where used
examples: A notification sender uses a retry policy.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Composition builds behavior by delegating to collaborators. Inheritance is useful for genuine substitutable types, not merely sharing implementation. Prefer a clear has-a relationship when behavior varies independently.

workedExample.scenario: A notification sender uses a retry policy.
steps: It delegates retry decisions.
It does not become a subclass of RetryPolicy.

commonMistakes: Shared code alone is not evidence of an is-a relationship.
guidedExercise: Compare inheritance and delegation for notifications
material.independentExercise: Compose a session service from generator, hasher, and repository.
recallQuestions: Is this a has-a or is-a relationship?
Which behavior varies independently?

acceptanceCriteria: Delegation relationships are explicit
Inheritance is justified by substitutability where used

topics.title: Dependency inversion
topics.description: Important policy should not depend on incidental implementation details.
learningGoals: Domain policy compiles without framework imports
A fake satisfies the same behavioral contract
examples: Token rotation depends on a token-store contract.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Important policy should not depend on incidental implementation details. Define a contract at an actual boundary and supply the concrete dependency at construction. This enables testing policy without importing the framework or database.

workedExample.scenario: Token rotation depends on a token-store contract.
steps: An in-memory store supports unit tests.
A JDBC adapter supplies persistence later.

commonMistakes: Dependency inversion is not a requirement for an interface per class.
guidedExercise: Identify the policy and infrastructure sides
material.independentExercise: Run a use case with manual constructor wiring and a fake store.
recallQuestions: Which side owns the contract?
Where is the concrete adapter chosen?

acceptanceCriteria: Domain policy compiles without framework imports
A fake satisfies the same behavioral contract

topics.title: Entity
topics.description: An entity represents a thing whose identity remains meaningful as its state changes.
learningGoals: Identity remains stable through transitions
Mutable values do not define entity identity
examples: Account A changes from ACTIVE to FROZEN.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: An entity represents a thing whose identity remains meaningful as its state changes. Decide which operations preserve invariants and which identity defines equality. Persistence annotations are not what make an object an entity.

workedExample.scenario: Account A changes from ACTIVE to FROZEN.
steps: Its balance and identity persist.
Another account with the same balance remains different.

commonMistakes: Matching all field values does not necessarily make two entities identical.
guidedExercise: Define account identity separately from balance
material.independentExercise: Create a Session entity whose token history can change without changing session identity.
recallQuestions: What survives a state change?
How should entity equality work?

acceptanceCriteria: Identity remains stable through transitions
Mutable values do not define entity identity

topics.title: Value objects

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: A value object is defined by its values rather than a separate lifecycle identity.
learningGoals: Invalid values cannot be constructed
Equality and normalization policies are tested

material.explanation: A value object is defined by its values rather than a separate lifecycle identity. Validate it at construction and prefer immutability. Replace a value when it changes rather than exposing unrestricted setters.

steps: Two equivalent amounts in the same currency compare by the chosen policy.
Different currencies cannot be added silently.

commonMistakes: A primitive amount alone omits the currency and rounding contract.
material.independentExercise: Model CouponCode with an explicit normalization policy.
recallQuestions: What makes this a value rather than an entity?
Where should normalization happen?

acceptanceCriteria: Invalid values cannot be constructed
Equality and normalization policies are tested

topics.title: Domain service
topics.description: A domain service holds a domain operation that does not naturally belong to one entity.
learningGoals: The policy uses domain concepts only
Entity invariants remain enforced by entities
examples: A transfer policy evaluates two accounts and a limit.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: A domain service holds a domain operation that does not naturally belong to one entity. Keep it focused on business decisions rather than HTTP or persistence orchestration. First check whether an existing entity already owns the needed information.

workedExample.scenario: A transfer policy evaluates two accounts and a limit.
steps: Accounts still own debit and credit invariants.
The use case manages atomic persistence.

commonMistakes: A domain service should not become a dumping ground for displaced entity behavior.
material.independentExercise: Design a transfer policy while keeping each account responsible for valid balances.
recallQuestions: Why does no single entity own this rule?
What infrastructure should this service avoid?

acceptanceCriteria: The policy uses domain concepts only
Entity invariants remain enforced by entities

topics.title: Application service
topics.description: An application service coordinates a use case: obtain inputs, load state, invoke domain behavior, persist, and return an outcome.
learningGoals: The use case has an explicit success and failure flow
Domain validation is not duplicated in callers

tasks.title: Explain Application service in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: An application service coordinates a use case: obtain inputs, load state, invoke domain behavior, persist, and return an outcome. It defines orchestration and atomic boundaries while delegating domain rules to their owners.

steps: Load and validate domain state.
Persist revocation and replacement together, then return issuance data.

commonMistakes: A controller should not contain the entire use-case algorithm.
guidedExercise: Trace orchestration separately from token rules
material.independentExercise: Implement a withdrawal coordinator using an in-memory repository.
recallQuestions: What belongs to orchestration?
Which domain rules should it delegate?

acceptanceCriteria: The use case has an explicit success and failure flow
Domain validation is not duplicated in callers

topics.title: Interface design
topics.description: Design an interface from concrete caller needs.
learningGoals: Every operation is justified by a caller
Atomicity and absence semantics are documented
examples: A rotation store exposes an atomic claim operation.

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words
Work through a concrete example
Check a boundary or failure case

material.explanation: Design an interface from concrete caller needs. Specify absence, errors, atomic operations, and ownership of returned data. Do not expose generic CRUD methods when they weaken an invariant the use case needs to preserve.

workedExample.scenario: A rotation store exposes an atomic claim operation.
steps: The result identifies whether this caller won.
Separate read and write methods cannot promise the same concurrency behavior.

commonMistakes: A broad repository interface can hide a missing atomicity contract.
guidedExercise: Write callers before finalizing the interface
material.independentExercise: Design a token repository without exposing raw tokens or arbitrary status setters.
recallQuestions: What guarantee does the caller require?
Which method makes an invalid sequence possible?

acceptanceCriteria: Every operation is justified by a caller
Atomicity and absence semantics are documented

topics.title: Fakes and behavioral contract tests

tasks.title: Explain the concept without notes
Complete the guided exercise
Verify the independent exercise

topics.description: A fake implements a useful simplified behavior for tests.
learningGoals: Important contract behavior matches across adapters
Tests assert outcomes rather than incidental call order
examples: A fake token store rejects a duplicate hash.

material.explanation: A fake implements a useful simplified behavior for tests. It must preserve the contract's important rules, or tests may approve behavior the real adapter cannot provide. Reuse a small contract test against multiple implementations when that boundary matters.

workedExample.scenario: A fake token store rejects a duplicate hash.
steps: The JDBC store must reject it too.
Both report absence consistently.

commonMistakes: A fake that always succeeds can conceal uniqueness and failure bugs.
guidedExercise: Test missing, duplicate, and successful lookup
material.independentExercise: Run the same repository behavior cases against two implementations.
recallQuestions: Which behavior can your fake safely simplify?
What discrepancy would invalidate a unit test?

acceptanceCriteria: Important contract behavior matches across adapters
Tests assert outcomes rather than incidental call order

exercises.description: Refactor working account behavior into justified responsibilities.
learningGoals: Refactor working account behavior into justified responsibilities.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.

tasks.title: deposit, withdraw, freeze, unfreeze, close
Closed account cannot transact
Frozen account cannot withdraw
Amount must be positive
Balance cannot go negative
Check boundary and failure cases
Verify: All state and amount rules have passing tests
Verify: The refactor preserves observable behavior
Verify: Callers cannot bypass balance or lifecycle rules
Verify: Every added class or interface has a concrete justification

requirements: Support deposit, withdraw, freeze, unfreeze, and close
Closed accounts cannot transact; frozen accounts cannot withdraw
For this exercise close requires zero balance
State changes follow a declared repeated-action policy
constraints: Start with a small procedural solution, then refactor
Plain Java; no framework imports in the domain
Introduce an interface only for a useful boundary
deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified

material.explanation: First prove the business rules with tests, then use those tests to protect a responsibility refactor. Keep balance and state invariants with the account. Explain what remains in the use-case coordinator rather than adding abstractions for appearance.

steps: Freeze prevents withdrawing 5.
Unfreeze allows it and leaves 15; closing rejects a nonzero balance.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Implement and test the rule table in a small solution.
Move invariant checks into meaningful account behavior.
Compare class responsibilities before and after.
material.independentExercise: Add a transfer use case and explain the cross-account invariant plus the eventual transaction boundary.

Why does each collaborator exist?

acceptanceCriteria: All state and amount rules have passing tests
The refactor preserves observable behavior
Callers cannot bypass balance or lifecycle rules
Every added class or interface has a concrete justification

tasks.title: Verify: Missing and duplicate behavior are explicit
Verify: The fake satisfies observable contract tests
Verify: Durability and concurrency limits are documented

exercises.description: Verify that fake and persistent adapters promise the same behavior.
learningGoals: Verify that fake and persistent adapters promise the same behavior.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: Saving a duplicate token hash is forbidden.
requirements: Define a minimal lookup-and-save contract from a caller
Specify missing IDs, duplicate business keys, and failure behavior
Create an in-memory adapter now; describe the persistent adapter for Module 5
Do not claim durability or cross-process atomicity from the fake
constraints: Plain Java tests; PostgreSQL implementation comes in Module 5
deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified

material.explanation: A fake is useful only when its simplified behavior preserves the contract relevant to the use case. Explicitly label its limits. Reuse the same observable cases when the JDBC adapter is introduced rather than replacing the contract with database-specific methods.

workedExample.scenario: Saving a duplicate token hash is forbidden.
steps: The fake rejects the second save.
The later JDBC adapter must reject the same business case.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Write the caller and minimum interface.
material.independentExercise: Deliberately weaken the fake to always accept duplicates and show which contract test detects it.
recallQuestions: What can the fake simplify?
What guarantee must the real adapter prove separately?

examples: The application service obtains a token and session.
